gotcha_text: Landlords often insert clauses that hold founders personally liable for the entire lease term, regardless of business failure. This allows them to pierce the corporate veil and seize personal assets like homes or savings if the startup fails.
fix_text: Tenant Pulse identifies unbounded personal obligations and suggests language to trigger a release of liability after a set period. It provides the precise legal leverage needed to transition from a personal guarantee to a corporate-only obligation.
deep_dive_html:
For tech founders, the personal guarantee is the single most dangerous provision in a commercial lease. While landlords view these as essential security for unproven entities, an improperly drafted clause can strip away the very protections of the corporate veil that the startup was built to maintain.

The Trap: Unconditional and Uncapped Liability

The primary danger lies in the "unconditional" nature of many standard-form guarantees. In these scenarios, the landlord is not required to pursue the corporate entity's assets before coming after the founder's personal bank accounts or real estate. Without specific limitations, the guarantor remains on the hook for the entire lease term, including future rent, unamortized tenant improvements, and even legal fees incurred during an eviction. This creates a permanent drag on the founder's personal net worth that can jeopardize future fundraising rounds or personal solvency.

  • No Notice Requirement: The landlord may be able to trigger a default without notifying the guarantor personally.
  • Full Term Exposure: The guarantee does not expire even if the business pivots or downsizes.
  • Cross-Default Triggers: A default on a separate loan could potentially trigger a default under the lease guarantee.

The Market-Standard Defense

Sophisticated tenants do not simply accept personal liability; they negotiate structured exits. The gold standard is the "Good Guy Guarantee" (GGG). This provision limits the guarantor's liability to the period during which the tenant occupies the premises and provides formal notice of intent to vacate. Once the premises are surrendered in good condition, the personal liability ceases. This allows a founder to walk away from a failing lease without being tethered to the remaining years of the term.

Another vital strategy is the "Burn-Off" clause. This allows the personal guarantee to expire after a predetermined period—typically 24 to 36 months—provided the tenant has maintained a clean payment history. This rewards the startup's growing creditworthiness and protects the founder's long-term solvency. Furthermore, negotiating a "Cap" on the guarantee—limiting it to a specific dollar amount or a set number of months of rent—can prevent the landlord from claiming massive amounts for unamortized costs.
